newsitem.title: USA: Academic, Fed official eyed for Fed Board - source.
newsitem.headline: Academic, Fed official eyed for Fed Board - source.

text.p: An academic and a long-time Federal Reserve official are among the candidates being considered for the two vacant governor positions at the central bank's Board, according to sources close to the Fed.

"Christina Romer is a well-regarded economist. A woman, for sure, will show up on that list," a source told Reuters. "Edwin Truman, the Director of the International Division at the Fed Board, is also being considered."
Romer, 38, is a professor of economics at the University of California at Berkeley, and holds a PhD from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Janet Yellen, a former Berkeley economics professor, left the Fed to head the White House's Council of Economic Advisers.
The other Fed governor's empty seat was held by Lawrence Lindsey who is leaving to join the American Entreprise Institute.
Truman, 55, holds a PhD from Yale University and has been in the international division of the Fed since 1972.
The source, however, did not expect the White House to announce its Fed appointees any time soon.
"They are at the early stage in making a long list. The White House has a history of moving slowly on this," the source added.

President Clinton, who already appointed two of the seven Fed Board members -- Vice Chair Alice Rivlin and Governor Laurence Meyer -- may have the rare opportunity of nominating three more governors in the first year of his second term.
The governor's mandate currently filled by Susan Phillips, ends in January 1998, the source said.
Phillips' departure would leave only two Republican appointees at the Fed Board -- Chairman Alan Greenspan and Governor Edward Kelley.
Romer is known for a 1996 paper, "Federal Reserve Private Information and the Behavior of Interest Rates," she co-authored with her husband, economist David Romer.
The Romers' paper shows markets' overreaction stems from the fact -- often suspected in the marketplace -- that the Fed has more information about inflation than private forecasters.

It concluded that, "The Federal Reserve does appear to possess information about the current and future state of the economy that is not known to market participants... that there is important asymmetric information betwen the Federal Reserve and the public."

Another source close to the Fed, who also saw Romer and Truman as likely candidates, said the paper drew attention at the Fed which was concerned about the markets' reaction to its 1994 preemptive tightening cycle.
Like Yellen, Romer resides within the San Francisco Fed district. Her appointment would not conflict with a Fed rule that requires each of the seven Board members to represent a different district.
The first source said Truman has often advised Greenspan on international affairs and is among the most knowledgeable Fed officials in terms of the operations of foreign central banks.
"Truman is also well regarded at the Treasury," the source said, noting that Treasury Deputy Secretary Lawrence Summers has voiced support for Truman in White House circles.
The second source noted that Truman's role at the Fed has gained prominence in recent years due to globalization and closer ties between major central banks.
Though he would not have the familiarity that Lindsey, whose governor's term ends in 2000, had with U.S. banking issues, he would bring a global view to the Fed, the source said.
Truman's nomination would not be a concern in terms of Fed rules since, like Lindsey, he would represent the Richmond Fed district.
Neither Romer nor Truman could be immediately contacted for comment.
